nodes.text: If you then will not lose heart,
do nothing more with the basin:
pour onto the stone that stands there
some of the spring with it.
Truly, then you will have good luck
if you come away from there with honour.
The wild man directed me there
along a path to the left hand.
I went that way and found
the truth of what he had said,
just as he had told me.
I found great splendour there.
One will never more hear,
whether the world stands short or long,
such delightful birdsong
as I heard at the linden
when I came riding up to it.
Anyone who had ever been
a man sorrowing unto death,
his heart would have been gladdened there.
It was so strewn with birds
that I lost sight of the branches
and saw little of the leaves either.
No two of them were in any way alike;
their song was just as varied,
high and low.
Their voices were given back to them
with an equal echo by the forest.
How song answered song there!
I saw the spring beneath it,
and all that the wild man had told me of.
The stone was an emerald;
from every corner shone
a ruby so bright
the morning star could not be
more beautiful when it rises
and the haze of the air lets it through.
When I found the basin hanging,
I thought at once:
since I was riding in search of adventure,
it would be unmanly
if I then refrained
from testing what it was.
And my unwise mind advised me,
which very often does me harm,
to pour onto the stone.
Then the sun that had been shining went out,
and the birdsong ceased,
as a heavy storm forced it.
The clouds began
in that same moment
to rise in the four quarters;
the bright day was made such
that I could scarcely see the linden.
Great misfortune happened here.
Very soon I saw
on all sides around me
a good thousand thousand flashes of lightning;
after them struck just as often
a thunderclap so mighty
that I lay on the ground.
A hail and a rain arose;
had not God's blessing
preserved me from the peril of the storm,
I would have been dead many times over in that while.
The storm became so violent
that it broke down the forest.
